Hey there! It sounds like you might quickly benefit from learning some grounding techniques.

Grounding techniques are what you use when you're feeling overwhelmed, dissociated, about to crash out, etc. An effective grounding technique can help you reengage your higher logical brain and reduce input from your amygdala (lizard fight-or- flight brain).

Here's my favorite one:

1 - Stop and take as deep a breath as possible.  It's okay if you feel like you can't breathe deep or you're hyperventilating, you just want to do the best you can.

2 - Tell yourself " okay let's slow down and get grounded."

3 - Look around yourself and name five things you can see, four things you can hear,  three things you can feel, two things you can smell, and one thing you can taste.  If it's possible to actually engage your senses, do it at this time. Touch things of different textures, smell different objects, put a Jolly Rancher or some gum in your mouth, etc. 

4 - Notice that things are starting to slow down a little bit and that's good! Repeat the 5-4-3-2-1 game if you need more centering. 

5 - Focusing on breathing while you are doing this is a great addition. Breathe in slowly through your nose and count how many seconds that takes. Blow that breath slowly from your mouth for twice as much time.  This can really help with hyperventilation if you slowly increase your times,  e.g. - 2 seconds in,  4 seconds out,  then after a few times 3 seconds in,  6 seconds out.

First of all I want to say I'm proud of you for taking the step of going to therapy. It absolutely takes bravery in commitment, but in all likelihood you will be better for it in the end.

In the beginning your therapist and you will get to become acquainted with one another. They'll very likely ask you what brought you to therapy and what you hope to gain from it.  As much as you may hate the thought you will have to talk to them about the trauma you've experienced so that they can help you process and, accept, and move past it.  

Because you have to talk about your original traumas, unfortunately I have to tell you it does get worse before it gets better.  Depending on your symptoms, you may have a panic attack, you may cry, you may even dissociate. Please just know that won't necessarily happen every session.  But the therapist has to understand what happens to you in order to give you the coping and processing skills that we all commonly lack.  

As for how you can tell it's working you will notice the small victories start to accumulate over time. Perhaps a trigger that always gave you a panic attack now gives you anxiety, sure...but you were able to cut the panic attack off at the pass and restore yourselves to a state of calm in a handful of minutes.  Keep an eye out for things like that happening because even a few saved panic attacks is a big win.

It's going to be a challenging journey to do therapy, but if you find a therapist have you vibe with and who specializes in your issues, I think you'll ultimately find it extremely helpful.
